Supporters assume disclosed evaluations are honest and that disclosure does not itself leak hazardous details.

choice.p: Labs already publish model cards voluntarily. Why do supporters want disclosure to be mandatory and standardized?
o: Voluntary cards vary in timing and content; standard ones let outsiders compare models
Voluntary model cards break trade secret law unless a statute requires them
Mandatory cards would let the government approve each model before release
Standard cards would remove the need for labs to run their own dangerous-capability tests at all
ow: Labs publish voluntary cards legally today.
Disclosure mandates require documentation, not pre-approval.
Model cards report test results; they don't replace testing.

items.p: A law would require AI developers to publish model cards with dangerous-capability test results at release. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: compelled disclosure is speech regulation and may fail First Amendment review, especially when it requires judgments rather than facts (Sokhansanj and Arnold, Lawfare; xAI's suit against a California disclosure law); self-reported evaluations miss flaws outsiders find (Longpre et al.); detailed results can spread hazardous information (the reason the EU allows redacted summaries).
keys: First Amendment risk (Sokhansanj and Arnold; xAI lawsuit)
Self-reported tests give limited assurance (Longpre et al.)
Detailed results can leak hazardous information
items.x: Under the EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, the full safety report goes to the EU AI Office and the public version can be redacted. Longpre et al. propose protected third-party flaw disclosure to address the self-reporting problem.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring model cards with dangerous-capability test results?
o: Detailed results can spread hazardous information
Model cards would reveal users' private chat histories to the public
Disclosure would let the FTC block new model releases at will
Model cards are far too short to be useful to anyone reading them
ow: Model cards describe the model, not users' chats.
Disclosure mandates require publication, not FTC approval.
Critics focus on legal risk, self-reporting and hazards, not length.

items.p: Match each model-disclosure variant to the proposal or law that uses it.
pairs: FTC-enforced consumer and safety model cards
AI Systems Transparency Act (Coons, Britt, Schatz, Lankford)
Full report to a regulator, redacted public summary
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
Model access a fixed time before release
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (45-day access)
Public transparency report at each new model's release
California SB 53
items.x: Consumer-protection model cards cover more models but go shallower on catastrophic risk, while confidential reports to a regulator reduce trade-secret and hazard concerns. Researchers led by Shayne Longpre propose a further variant: protected reporting of flaws by outside researchers.

items.p: Under California SB 53 and similar state laws, what kinds of events count as a 'critical safety incident' that must be reported? Name two.
items.answer: Any two of: unauthorized access to or theft of model weights that causes death or injury; harm from a catastrophic risk materializing; loss of control of a model that causes death or injury; a model using deceptive techniques to evade its developer's controls in a way that shows materially increased catastrophic risk.
keys: Theft of or unauthorized access to model weights (causing harm)
Harm from a catastrophic risk
Loss of control of a model (causing harm)
Model deceptively evading developer controls
items.x: Critics such as Arnold and Llerena (LawAI) note that three of the four categories require actual harm. Under SB 53, reports go to the Office of Emergency Services confidentially, and anonymized annual summaries start in 2027.

choice.p: Which of these counts as a 'critical safety incident' under California SB 53?
o: A model deceptively evading its developer's controls in a way that shows higher catastrophic risk
A chatbot giving a user incorrect medical advice that delays their treatment for a serious illness
A data breach that exposes customers' names and email addresses to hackers
A new model scoring much higher than expected on a public coding benchmark
ow: SB 53's categories concern catastrophic risk, not ordinary product errors.
Customer data breaches fall under other laws.
A benchmark result is not an incident under SB 53.

items.p: Match each regime to its AI incident reporting deadline.
pairs: California SB 53
15 days to the Office of Emergency Services; 24 hours to an appropriate authority if death or serious injury is imminent
New York RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315
72 hours
EU General-Purpose AI Code of Practice
2 to 15 days depending on incident type
AI Kill Switch Act (House bill)
15-day reports to the Department of Homeland Security
items.x: The pacing.tech appendix lists an 'incident reporting deadline' as one transparency intervention, citing SB 53. As of Oct 2026 the AI Kill Switch Act (H.R. 9917, Reps. Lieu and Moran) has not passed; it was referred to committee in July 2026. The New York and Illinois deadlines apply from 2027.

items.p: State laws require frontier developers to report 'critical safety incidents' within days. Name two gaps or objections critics point to.
items.answer: Examples: three of four incident categories require actual harm, so OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face breach arguably need not be reported under SB 53 (Arnold and Llerena, LawAI); SB 53's deception category excludes behavior during evaluations designed to elicit it (Pebblous); without standard fields and several reporting channels, incident data stays fragmented (Dixon and Frase, CSET).
keys: Harm requirement misses serious near misses (Arnold and Llerena)
Deception during evaluations designed to elicit it is excluded (Pebblous)
Data fragmented without standard fields and channels (CSET)
items.x: Arnold and Llerena propose covering serious events without harm and nonpublic models. CSET proposes a hybrid system.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics point to in state laws requiring frontier developers to report 'critical safety incidents'?
o: Most incident types require actual harm, so serious near misses may go unreported
The laws require reports within minutes of an incident, a deadline that no company can meet
Reports go straight to the public, exposing companies' trade secrets to their competitors
The laws cover only open-weight models, leaving closed frontier models out of the reporting rules
ow: SB 53 allows 15 days (24 hours for imminent danger); New York and Illinois allow 72 hours.
SB 53 reports are confidential, with anonymized annual summaries.
The laws cover large frontier developers generally.

items.p: Why might an AI incident reporting system need voluntary reports from individuals and citizen reports from the public, journalists and watchdogs, as well as mandatory reports from companies?
items.answer: Mandatory reporting only captures incidents within its legal scope, and each channel alone leaves gaps. Voluntary reports from individuals and groups, and citizen reports from the public, journalists and watchdogs, capture incidents the mandatory system misses, giving fuller and more representative data on AI harms.
keys: Mandatory reports miss incidents outside their legal scope
Each channel alone has gaps; together they give fuller data
items.x: This 'hybrid' design was proposed by Ren Bin Lee Dixon and Heather Frase of CSET (Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology) in March 2024. They note that healthcare's reliance on voluntary reporting led to missing incidents. They want all three channels under one federal framework with a standardized classification system, warning that uneven state or domain-specific standards make aggregate incident data unreliable.

choice.p: Why might an AI incident reporting system need voluntary and citizen reports as well as mandatory company reports?
o: Mandatory reports miss incidents outside their scope; voluntary and citizen reports fill the gaps
Mandatory reporting violates the First Amendment, so only voluntary reports are allowed
Companies already report everything, so citizen reports are needed only for small firms
A hybrid system would let each state keep its own separate incident reporting format
ow: In a hybrid system, mandatory reporting stays one of the channels.
The worry is that mandatory reporting misses incidents, not that it reports everything.
The proposal puts all channels under one federal framework with standard classification.

items.p: Proposals would extend oversight to internal deployment (labs' use of models inside the company). Match each proposal to the gap it targets.
pairs: Internal-use risk reports
Regulators never hear about risks from models used only inside the lab
Tiered internal access rules
Any staff member can use the most capable internal model for anything
Disclosure of AI's role in building a model
Outsiders can't tell how much AI research is automated or goes unreviewed
Power to restrict or suspend internal use
A dangerous internal model keeps running with no outside check
items.x: Sources: a risk report each time a substantially more capable model goes into internal use, from IAPS (Delaney, O'Brien et al.); tripwires, tiered internal access rules and an internal oversight board from Apollo Research (Stix, Hobbhahn et al.); disclosure on NIST's request in the Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act; powers to verify, restrict or suspend internal use in the FRONTIER Act. California's SB 53 already requires large frontier developers to send the state confidential summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use, every three months by default.

items.p: Policies would extend oversight, reporting or limits to the AI models labs use internally, including for automating AI research. Name one concern or objection that has been raised.
items.answer: Examples: disclosing internal capabilities, usage and safeguards carries security and competitive risks to weigh for each type of information, so some details may suit private reports to government more than public release (Charnock, Moreno, Miller and Anderson, who still favor disclosure); if US labs pace themselves, China may not wait (economist Christian Catalini, on the 2026 employee letter).
keys: Disclosure has security and competitive costs to weigh (Charnock et al.)
US labs pacing themselves could cede ground to China (Catalini)
items.x: From the other side, Joe Kwon and Stephen Casper argue current laws still leave internal deployment under-covered because of scope ambiguity, point-in-time checks and information asymmetry.

choice.p: Which of these is a concern raised about extending oversight to the AI models labs use internally?
o: Disclosing internal capabilities and usage can create security and competitive risks
Internal models are too weak to matter for safety, so oversight is wasted
Internal oversight would force labs to open-source their models
Courts have ruled that a lab's internal use of AI is protected speech
ow: Advocates and critics alike treat internal models as often the most capable.
Oversight proposals involve reports and access, not open-sourcing.
No such ruling is cited.

items.p: What are AI companies' 'model behavior specifications', and why might requiring companies to publish them matter more as AI takes over more AI research?
items.answer: They set out the values, principles and norms a model is trained to follow, such as OpenAI's Model Spec and Anthropic's constitution for Claude. Published specs help outsiders understand a model's alignment and behavior while it is doing AI research and development.
keys: Documents stating the values, principles and norms a model is trained to follow
Examples: OpenAI's Model Spec, Anthropic's constitution for Claude
Help outsiders understand a model's alignment and behavior while it does AI R&D
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report asks Congress to require publishing them, one of four kinds of transparency it wants legislated, with risk management for automated AI research, incident reporting and whistleblower protections. IFP says bills already introduced (the FRONTIER Act, AI Incident Reporting Act, AI Whistleblower Protection Act) would cover much of the other three, but publishing specs would need new legislation.

choice.p: What is an AI company's 'model behavior specification'?
o: A document setting out the values and rules a model is trained to follow
A technical sheet listing a model's size, training compute and test scores
A lab's plan for which risk thresholds trigger extra safety measures
A contract stating what customers may and may not use the model for
ow: That describes parts of a model card; a behavior specification describes how the model is meant to behave.
That is a frontier AI framework, which California's SB 53 already requires large frontier developers to publish.
That is a usage policy for customers; a behavior specification governs the model's own conduct.

lessons.title: Compute, race tempo and AI-use records

items.p: As of October 2026, is there a US federal requirement to report large AI training runs to the government? What existed before?
items.answer: No. Biden's Executive Order 14110 (2023) used the Defense Production Act to require such reports, and Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security proposed quarterly reporting rules in September 2024, but the order was revoked in January 2025.
keys: No current federal requirement
EO 14110 required reports (2023)
Revoked January 2025
items.x: State laws such as SB 53 use 10^26 operations only to define who is covered. A June 2026 executive order set up only a voluntary framework for pre-release government testing. By contrast, the EU AI Act (Article 52) requires providers to notify the European Commission within two weeks once a model crosses its 10^25 systemic-risk threshold.

choice.p: As of October 2026, which best describes US federal reporting of large AI training runs?
o: None now: Biden's 2023 order required reports but was revoked in January 2025
Developers must notify Commerce within two weeks of crossing 10^26 operations
The FRONTIER Act now requires quarterly training-run reports to the Commerce Department
A June 2026 executive order requires reports for every training run above 10^25 operations
ow: Two-week notice after crossing a threshold is the EU AI Act's rule, at 10^25.
The FRONTIER Act is a bill in House committee, not law.
The June 2026 order created a voluntary pre-release testing framework, not training-run reporting.

items.p: Governments would require developers to report training runs above a fixed compute threshold. Name one objection critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, since data quality, post-training and efficiency gains also drive capability, so fixed thresholds can miss risky models (Cohere's policy primer 'The Limits of Thresholds' and Sara Hooker); quarterly reporting is too burdensome, so make it annual or semiannual (CCIA, US Chamber of Commerce).
keys: Compute is an imperfect proxy for risk (Cohere, Sara Hooker)
Reporting burden too high (CCIA, US Chamber)
items.x: Heim and Koessler, who support thresholds, reply that compute works best as an initial filter for further scrutiny, updated over time and paired with capability-based measures.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics raise to requiring reports of training runs above a fixed compute threshold?
o: Compute is an imperfect proxy for risk, so fixed thresholds can miss risky models
Reporting would expose the personal data of the model's users to regulators
Reports would let foreign governments track and seize US chips abroad
Thresholds are set so low that they cover every small AI startup
ow: Training-run reports concern compute and models, not user data.
Critics raise no such claim.
Critics stress the opposite problem: efficiency gains let risky models fall below fixed thresholds.

items.p: Some proposals would have labs report how their compute is split across uses such as final training runs, experiments, internal use and serving customers. What could this show that reports on single training runs miss?
items.answer: How much of a lab's compute goes into building its next models (experiments and internal use, increasingly by AI agents doing research) versus serving the public. That tracks the scale of internal R&D and its automation, which a per-run training threshold does not capture.
keys: Share of compute spent building next models vs serving customers
Tracks internal R&D and automation
Per-run thresholds don't capture it
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report lists such breakdowns among information that would help outsiders understand automated AI R&D, and notes that leading labs now use more compute developing next-generation models than serving today's AI. The pacing.tech research agenda lists the item as a lever, citing Epoch (2026) and Biden's Executive Order 14110, with the caveat that listing a lever is not an argument for using it.

choice.p: What could reports of how a lab splits its compute (training runs, experiments, internal use, serving customers) show that single training-run reports miss?
o: How much compute goes to building the next models versus serving users
Which of the lab's customers are using its models for dangerous or prohibited purposes
Whether each of the lab's models has passed its dangerous-capability tests
How much the lab pays for electricity at each of its data centers
ow: Compute splits are aggregate shares, not customer identities.
Test results come from evaluations and model cards, not compute splits.
Compute splits measure how compute is used, not energy prices.

items.p: In one well-known game-theory model of AI races, how can better information about rivals' capabilities make a race more dangerous?
o: When teams are close, it removes uncertainty that would make them cautious
It reveals rivals' safety methods, so teams start copying each other's risky shortcuts
It lets governments pick winners early, which provokes the losing teams into rushing ahead
It sets off stock market swings that push the labs to rush out their next releases
ow: The model's mechanism is about uncertainty and caution, not copying methods.
The model involves competing teams, not government picking winners.
The model's mechanism does not run through financial markets.
keys: Applies when teams are close
Removes the uncertainty that induces caution
items.x: The model is Armstrong, Bostrom and Shulman's 'Racing to the Precipice'. The pacing.tech research agenda cites it and treats the wider question (when common knowledge of progress intensifies or weakens races) as open. It separately lists lead-margin reporting (months between the top lab and the next) as a lever, with the caveat that listing a lever is not an argument for using it.

items.p: In August 2026 the National Archives (NARA) issued guidance applying the Federal Records Act to AI prompts and outputs. Under that guidance, why might many officials' AI chats never become federal records?
items.answer: The guidance treats AI material as not necessarily received by an agency until it is downloaded or captured in an agency system, so chats left on a vendor's platform may not count as records.
keys: Material counts only once downloaded or captured in an agency system
Chats left on a vendor's platform may not count as records
items.x: Asad Ramzanali and Margaret Mullins of the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator criticized this as narrower than NARA's past guidance on cloud records and electronic messages, and noted it omits chain-of-thought, metadata and procurement terms. They say closing the gap now depends on agencies, courts and Congress being willing to say the guidance is not enough. As of Oct 2026 no statute specifically addresses AI records.

choice.p: Under NARA's August 2026 guidance, why might many officials' AI chats never become federal records?
o: Material left on a vendor's platform isn't treated as received until captured
It orders agencies to delete all of their AI chat records after 30 days to save storage
It bans federal employees from using AI tools for any official work
It covers only the Defense Department and the intelligence agencies
ow: The guidance orders no such deletion; the problem is that some material is never captured.
The guidance doesn't ban AI use; it addresses how AI material is kept.
The Federal Records Act guidance applies to federal agencies generally.

units.title: Verification and oversight
units.desc: Who checks what AI labs say: audits, embedded evaluators, government testing, certified verifiers, licensing and dedicated regulators.

items.p: As of October 2026, which US state has enacted the first mandatory annual audit of frontier AI developers, and when do audits begin?
items.answer: Illinois, through SB 315 (Public Act 104-0538), signed in July 2026. Annual audits begin January 1, 2028 (or 90 days after a developer first qualifies, if later).
keys: Illinois SB 315
Audits begin January 1, 2028
items.x: Massachusetts, Michigan and Pennsylvania bills and the federal FRONTIER Act copy the idea. The voluntary White House Accord on Super Intelligence (Sept 29, 2026) recommends an independent external auditor but is not legally binding.

o: Illinois, through SB 315 (signed July 2026); annual audits begin January 1, 2028
California, through SB 53 (in force January 2026); annual audits begin January 1, 2027
Michigan, through HB 4668 (frontier developer bill); annual audits begin January 1, 2027
Massachusetts, through S.3228 (2026); audits every 120 days begin in 2027
ow: SB 53 requires published frameworks and incident reports but no third-party audit.
Michigan's audit bill had not been enacted as of Oct 2026.
The Massachusetts Senate text had not been enacted as of Oct 2026, so it is not law.

items.p: Frontier AI audit proposals differ in what the auditor checks. What separates a 'framework compliance audit' (Illinois SB 315) from 'independent catastrophic-risk evaluations' (Massachusetts Senate text S.3228)?
o: Compliance audits check a lab follows its own framework; evaluations have outsiders test its models for each catastrophic risk
A compliance audit is carried out by government staff, while independent evaluations are run by the lab's own internal safety team
A compliance audit covers only open-weight models; independent evaluations cover only the closed models that labs sell through an API
A compliance audit happens before training begins; independent evaluations happen only after a reported incident
ow: Both rely on outside parties; neither variant is defined by government versus self-assessment.
Neither variant is defined by open versus closed weights.
Neither is tied to before training or after incidents.
items.x: Under S.3228 the evaluations would happen every 120 days. Critics note the compliance version does not judge whether the framework itself is adequate, so a weak framework can pass a clean audit. Substantive testing adds that check at higher cost.
keys: Compliance audit: checks the lab follows its own framework
Independent evaluations: outsiders test top models for each catastrophic risk

items.p: A law requires frontier AI developers to hire an independent auditor each year to check their safety practices. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: premature, because the auditing ecosystem does not exist yet and models change faster than audits can be done (NetChoice); requires private actors to make highly subjective judgments (TechNet); audits can become a checkbox exercise without high standards and deep access (Brundage et al., themselves supporters); qualified auditors are scarce and hired away by labs (Fortune).
keys: Ecosystem not ready, models change too fast (NetChoice)
Subjective determinations (TechNet)
Risk of checkbox audits (Brundage et al.)
Talent shortage and poaching by labs (Fortune)
items.x: The authors of the 'Frontier AI Auditing' paper (Brundage et al.) respond by proposing standards and graded assurance levels, so policy can demand more rigorous audits as risk rises.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to mandatory annual audits of frontier AI developers?
o: The audit field isn't ready: auditors are scarce and models outpace audits
Audits would force labs to publish their model weights online for anyone to download and inspect
Audits would replace each lab's own safety framework with a single framework written by government regulators
Audits would apply only to open-weight models, so closed frontier models escape any review
ow: Auditors get confidential access; no audit mandate requires publishing weights.
Compliance audits check the lab's own framework; the common critique runs the other way, that a weak framework can pass.
Audit mandates cover the largest developers however they release their models.

items.p: Why might rules for frontier AI audits define tiers of assurance, and what would separate the lowest tier from the highest?
items.answer: Tiers let policy demand more rigorous, deeper-access audits as risk rises. The lowest would be a time-limited audit of one system lasting a few weeks, mostly through API (black-box) access, which can catch errors but is less likely to detect fraud (deliberate deception); the highest would be continuous verification designed to detect active deception.
keys: Tiers let rigor and access scale with risk
Lowest: weeks-long audit mostly through API access, catches errors more than fraud
Highest: continuous verification built to detect deception
items.x: This is the 'AI Assurance Levels' scheme in 'Frontier AI Auditing' (Brundage, Anderljung et al., Jan 2026), running from AAL-1 to AAL-4; the authors call AAL-4 'treaty-grade'. They recommend AAL-1 as a baseline for frontier AI and AAL-2 (months long, gray-box or partial access to internals, internal documents, staff interviews) as a near-term goal for the most advanced developers, and say AAL-3 and AAL-4 are not yet technically and organizationally feasible.

choice.p: In a tiered scheme for frontier AI audits, what would separate the highest tier from the lowest?
o: Highest: continuous checks built to catch deception; lowest: a weeks-long audit via API
The highest is run by government inspectors; the lowest by the lab's own internal safety team
The highest covers open-weight models; the lowest covers only models that are sold through an API
The highest is required by state law; the lowest is set by voluntary industry commitments
ow: All tiers are outside audits; they differ in access, duration and confidence.
The tiers aren't defined by how a model is released.
The tiers are defined by rigor and access, not by which rule requires them.

items.p: Why might audits of frontier AI labs need to cover the whole organization as well as its public products? Name two reasons.
items.answer: Any two of: internal deployment of models never released can cause harm, and auditors may not know about it by default; strong product safeguards can be undone by weak weight security, since stolen weights run without them; a well-controlled flagship product can sit beside riskier systems elsewhere; parts that look safe alone may not be safe once combined into agents.
keys: Internal deployments that are never released
Weak weight security undoes product safeguards
Riskier systems elsewhere in the company
Safe parts may be unsafe once combined
items.x: This case is made in 'Frontier AI Auditing' (Brundage, Anderljung et al., 2026), which says audits should cover 'the full range of organization-level safety and security risks', including internal deployment, information security and safety decision-making. The authors conclude the company level is best for confident conclusions, though harder to audit.

choice.p: Why might audits of frontier AI labs need to cover the whole organization as well as its public products?
o: Harm can come from models used only inside the lab, and stolen weights run without product safeguards
The EU AI Office already audits every public product in full, so the rest of the company is the only gap left
Labs are legally barred from letting outside auditors test their public products
Company-wide audits are cheaper and faster than testing individual models
ow: The EU AI Office can request access to general-purpose models, but it does not audit every product; the reasons concern where risk sits.
No such bar exists; auditors routinely test public products through APIs.
Company-level audits are harder to do, not cheaper or faster.

items.p: Match each version of embedded AI auditing to where it appears.
pairs: State-designated onsite verifier at each large developer
Option under study in California executive order N-9-26
Standing government team supervising each developer
ARI federal blueprint, modeled on bank examiners
Paid embedded evaluation partnership
Anthropic with Accenture (Sept 2026)
items.x: As of Oct 2026 no jurisdiction requires embedded auditors. California's executive order asks for recommendations by November 16, 2026 on amending state law, including requiring onsite verifiers at large frontier developers. GovAI researchers have also proposed voluntary embedded assessments with quarterly reports (Sept 2026). ARI is Americans for Responsible Innovation.

items.p: Outside evaluators would work inside frontier AI labs with ongoing access. Name two concerns critics and analysts have raised.
items.answer: Examples: with weak access, few resources or no say in decisions, embedded evaluations may give a false sense of security, and voluntary versions are unlikely to be enough (Apollo Research); mandatory third-party evaluation can raise the risk of leaks and industrial espionage (pacing.tech authors); long-term residents may come to share the views of the lab staff they oversee.
keys: False sense of security if access is weak (Apollo)
Voluntary versions likely insufficient (Apollo)
Leak and espionage risk (pacing.tech)
Residents may adopt lab staff's views
items.x: Apollo's authors, who support embedded evaluations, argue they should eventually be legally required to fix the access problem. The last concern is a general critique with no single named author.

choice.p: Which of these is a concern analysts have raised about embedded evaluators working inside frontier AI labs?
o: With weak access or no influence on decisions, they may give a false sense of security
They would have to publish a lab's trade secrets in their public reports
They could only test models after public release, too late to help
They would duplicate CAISI's existing mandatory inspections inside every lab
ow: Designs keep findings confidential or summarized; leak risk is a concern, but publishing trade secrets is not proposed.
Seeing models before release is the main point of embedding evaluators.
CAISI's testing is voluntary and does not include inspections inside labs.

items.p: As of October 2026, how does US government pre-deployment testing of frontier AI models work?
items.answer: It is voluntary. The Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) at NIST tests models under voluntary agreements with five labs, and a June 2026 executive order (EO 14409) directs several agencies to design a voluntary framework giving government up to 30 days of access to covered models before release. No bill making testing mandatory has passed.
keys: Voluntary, run by CAISI at NIST
Agreements with five labs
June 2026 order: up to 30 days early access
No mandatory bill has passed
items.x: The June 2026 order (EO 14409) expressly disclaims mandatory licensing or preclearance. China has required a government security assessment before launching public generative AI services since 2023.

o: Voluntary: CAISI tests under deals with five labs; a June 2026 order seeks up to 30 days' access
Mandatory: under a May 2026 executive order, developers must give CAISI 90 days of access to each model before release
Mandatory: the AI Risk Evaluation Act requires Energy Department testing of each model before deployment
None exists: CAISI was abolished in 2025 and all frontier model testing moved over to the EU AI Office
ow: A draft order with 90 days of access was shelved in May 2026; the June order is voluntary and allows up to 30 days.
The Hawley-Blumenthal bill would do this, but it has not passed.
CAISI exists and runs voluntary testing; the EU AI Office has no role in US release decisions.

items.p: Which bill would bar deploying covered frontier AI models without first participating in a Department of Energy evaluation program?
o: The AI Risk Evaluation Act (Hawley and Blumenthal)
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (S. 5576)
California SB 53
The AI Systems Transparency Act (sponsored by Coons and Britt)
ow: Warner's bill would create a safety board inside the Commerce Department with 45 days of access before release.
SB 53 requires published frameworks and transparency reports, with no government testing gate.
This bill would have the FTC require model-card disclosures; it creates no government testing program.
items.x: The AI Risk Evaluation Act (S. 2938, introduced Sept 2025) would set up an evaluation program at the Department of Energy and require developers to provide information on request. It was still in committee as of Oct 2026. A guest post on the libertarian Cato Institute's blog (Juan Londono, Taxpayers Protection Alliance) called it a power grab by the executive, objecting mainly to a provision on oversight options up to nationalization.
keys: AI Risk Evaluation Act
Hawley and Blumenthal
Department of Energy evaluation program

items.p: Government evaluators would test frontier AI models for dangerous capabilities before release. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: evaluations can show a capability exists but not reliably that it is absent (Barnett et al., MIRI); a voluntary regime cannot bind labs that refuse (Mariana Olaizola Rosenblat); delaying access is not a durable cyber defense since comparable capabilities spread (Ji and Lohn, CSET); a mandatory window could block US releases (Trump, May 2026).
keys: Tests cannot prove absence of capability (MIRI)
Voluntary regime cannot bind (Rosenblat)
Delaying access is not a durable defense (CSET)
Could become a release blocker (Trump, May 2026)
items.x: In May 2026 Trump postponed signing a draft order that gave government 90 days of pre-launch access, saying it 'could have been a blocker'; Zuckerberg, Musk and David Sacks reportedly spoke with him first. The June 2026 order (EO 14409) instead directed agencies to design a voluntary framework with up to 30 days of access.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to government testing of frontier AI models before release?
o: Tests can show a model has a dangerous capability but can't reliably show it lacks one
Labs would have to publish their full model weights so that anyone could run the same tests
Tests would happen only after release, too late to stop a harmful launch
Testing duplicates the EU AI Office's pre-release approval of US models
ow: Pre-release testing gives government confidential access; none of these proposals requires publishing weights.
These proposals test models before release by design; critics question what the tests can show.
The EU AI Office can request access to models, but it is not a pre-release gate for US releases.

items.p: Why do rigorous AI audits need more than black-box access (only querying a model and reading its outputs)? Say what access to model internals and access to development information each let auditors do.
items.answer: White-box access to internals (weights, activations, gradients) lets auditors run stronger attacks, interpret how the model works, and fine-tune it to surface hidden capabilities. Outside-the-box access to training methods, code, data, documentation and internal evaluation results lets them examine the development process and design more targeted tests.
keys: White-box: internals such as weights and activations
Enables stronger attacks, interpretation, fine-tuning
Outside-the-box: training and deployment information
Lets auditors examine the process and target tests
items.x: The case is made in Casper et al., 'Black-Box Access is Insufficient for Rigorous AI Audits' (2024). Black-box access is how most audits of frontier systems had worked. The authors argue results depend on the access granted, so reports should disclose it, and they discuss technical, physical and legal safeguards to limit the security risk of deeper access.

choice.p: What does white-box access to a model's internals, such as its weights and activations, let auditors do that only querying it can't?
o: Run stronger attacks, interpret how the model works, and fine-tune it to find hidden abilities
Query the finished model through its public API as often as they like, free of charge
Read the lab's board minutes, investor agreements, customer contracts and other corporate records
Publish the model's weights openly for anyone to use once the audit has been completed
ow: Querying through an API is black-box access, the thing white-box access goes beyond.
White-box access means model internals such as weights and activations, not corporate records.
Deeper access calls for security safeguards; it doesn't mean publishing weights.

items.p: Risk: a lab releases a model with dangerous capabilities that its own internal tests missed or underestimated. Name two policies proposed to catch this.
items.answer: Examples: government pre-deployment testing; mandatory third-party audits or independent catastrophic-risk evaluations; embedded evaluators inside labs; deeper evaluator access to model internals; mandatory disclosure of dangerous-capability test results.
keys: Government pre-deployment testing
Third-party audits or evaluations
Embedded evaluators
Deeper evaluator access
Disclosure of test results
items.x: Longpre et al. argue in-house evaluation is not enough and call for flaw-disclosure programs with legal safe harbors so outside researchers can report problems. If the cause is a model hiding what it can do, elicitation budgets and sandbagging checks also apply.

choice.p: A lab releases a model with dangerous capabilities that its own tests missed. Which of these is a policy proposed to catch this?
o: Government testing of frontier models before release
Federal preemption of all state AI safety laws and audits
Tighter export controls on advanced AI chips
Mandatory watermarking of all AI-generated images and video
ow: Preemption decides which level of government sets rules; it adds no check on a lab's tests.
Export controls limit who gets compute; they add no check on a lab's testing.
Watermarking labels AI content; it doesn't test models for dangerous capabilities.

items.p: What is an 'independent verification organization' (IVO) system for AI, such as the one California created with SB 813 (signed Sept 2026)?
items.answer: The state designates or certifies private organizations (IVOs), independent of the companies they check, to assess AI models and systems against state requirements. Government sets the application rules and criteria and can suspend or terminate an IVO. Developers are not compelled to use one; proposals in this family often reward participation with a legal benefit.
keys: State certifies private verifiers
Verifiers must be independent of those assessed
Government can suspend or revoke them
Participation voluntary for developers
items.x: Under SB 813, California's Government Operations Agency must certify the first IVOs by January 1, 2028. As of Oct 2026, Connecticut has enacted a voluntary pilot and Ohio has a bill. The federal FRONTIER Act would instead require the very largest developers to retain a federally licensed IVO.

o: The state certifies independent private verifiers to assess AI, and developers may choose to use them
The state hires its own engineers to inspect every frontier AI model before it is released
Developers must register each model with the state and pay a yearly licensing fee before they can sell it
Developers certify their own models against state rules and file the results with a state agency each year
ow: IVOs are private organizations; government certifies and oversees them but doesn't do the testing.
That describes registration or licensing; using an IVO is voluntary and involves outside assessment.
Self-certification lacks the independence that defines an IVO.

items.p: Under a regulatory-markets design, government certifies private verifiers that developers choose and pay, often for liability protection. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: when developers pick and pay verifiers, competition pushes verifiers toward leniency (Gabriel Weil); the accredited-auditor ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice); government needs its own examination capacity to judge verifiers (ARI); the FRONTIER Act's preemption would apply at once while the verifier market takes years (ARI's Brad Carson).
keys: Race to leniency (Weil)
Ecosystem does not exist yet (NetChoice)
Government needs its own capacity to judge verifiers (ARI)
Oversight gap under FRONTIER preemption (ARI)
items.x: Weil's proposed fix is mandatory liability insurance, so insurers carry the cost of harms and compete to price risk accurately. ARI's fix is a hybrid where government examines developers itself and keeps the final judgment.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to regulatory markets, where developers choose and pay government-certified private verifiers?
o: Since developers pick and pay verifiers, competition can push them toward leniency
Verifiers would all have to be federal employees, which would slow the hiring of qualified staff for years
The approach bans developers from running any of their own internal safety tests on models
Certified verifiers could seize models that fail their assessments
ow: Verifiers in these designs are private organizations certified by government.
Developers keep running their own tests; verification is an added check.
Verifiers assess and certify; no design lets them seize models.

items.p: Match each law or proposal to its design for private AI verifiers.
pairs: California SB 813
State-certified verifiers that developers choose to use
FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)
Mandatory federally licensed verifier for the largest developers
ARI blueprint (Americans for Responsible Innovation)
Government examiners keep final judgment and accredit verifiers
California AB 1405
Registry of AI auditors with independence rules
items.x: These range from a light registry to a mandate. Critics note voluntary versions bind no one who declines.

items.p: New York's RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315 require large frontier developers to file disclosure statements before operating in the state. How does this 'registration' differ from licensing?
o: Registration means filing information, with no approval; licensing requires revocable permission to build or release a model
Registration requires a government safety test before every new model is released; licensing only requires paying an annual fee
Registration applies to individual AI engineers; licensing applies to the companies that employ them
Registration is enforced by federal agencies; licensing is enforced only by state attorneys general
ow: Registration involves no safety test or approval; licensing is the version with approval.
Professional licensing of engineers is a separate proposal (Chinmayi Sharma); state registration covers companies.
Both state registration laws are enforced by the states.
items.x: Registration aims at knowing who the frontier developers are so other rules can reach them. As of Oct 2026, approval-based licensing appears in the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar), and the June 2026 executive order disclaims mandatory licensing.
keys: Registration: file information, no approval needed
Licensing: permission to build or release that government can revoke

items.p: Proposals would require frontier AI developers to obtain a government license or charter before training or deploying top models. Name two objections critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: FDA-style approval, applied simplistically, would fit frontier AI poorly because the product is hard to define and harms are deeply uncertain (Daniel Carpenter and Carson Ezell); a guest post on Cato's blog called the Hawley-Blumenthal testing bill an executive power grab; the June 2026 executive order rejects mandatory licensing.
keys: Product hard to define, harms uncertain (Carpenter and Ezell)
Executive power grab (guest post on Cato's blog)
Administration disclaims licensing (June 2026 order)
items.x: Supporters argue disclosure and liability act after the fact, while a license lets government stop a dangerous model before it ships and gives leverage over a few high-value companies.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to requiring a government license before training or deploying frontier AI models?
o: FDA-style approval, applied simplistically, fits AI poorly: the product is hard to define, harms uncertain
Licenses would cover only open-weight models, leaving the closed frontier labs and their models unregulated
Licensing would require labs to publish their model weights for review
Licensing would hand all AI oversight to the fifty state governments instead of to Congress
ow: Licensing proposals target frontier developers however they release models.
Licensing makes release conditional on approval; it doesn't require publishing weights.
Licensing proposals such as the Ban ASI Act would create federal agencies.

items.p: Match each proposed or existing frontier AI regulator to its source.
pairs: Cabinet-level Department of AI
Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (Sanders, Casar)
Safety board inside the Commerce Department
Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act (S. 5576)
Commerce Under Secretary for AI Security
FRONTIER Act (Obernolte, Trahan)
Office inside a state financial regulator, funded by fees
New York's RAISE Act (Department of Financial Services)
items.x: Supporters of a dedicated regulator argue US oversight is split across voluntary CAISI testing, state attorneys general and agencies with no AI mandate, so nobody has both expertise and authority. The EU AI Office has enforced general-purpose model rules since August 2026.

items.p: Proposals would create a dedicated federal regulator for frontier AI. Name two objections or weaknesses critics have pointed to.
items.answer: Examples: Sen. Ted Cruz blocked Sen. Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act, saying it gives the board and Commerce too much authority; Dan Parshall (Canary Institute) notes the FRONTIER Act's Under Secretary would need no Senate confirmation and has no money appropriated; IFP says even the existing testing body, CAISI, is underfunded.
keys: Too much authority for the board and Commerce (Cruz)
No Senate confirmation, no appropriation (Parshall)
Existing capacity underfunded (IFP)
items.x: The pacing.tech authors list 'regulator capacity' as an intervention and note that the US government AI evaluator's nominal annual budget is less than some individual frontier researchers' salaries.

choice.p: Which of these is a weakness critics have pointed to in proposals for a dedicated federal frontier AI regulator?
o: A new office with no Senate-confirmed head and no money appropriated may be too weak
A federal regulator would need each state's formal approval before it could act within that state
A federal regulator would automatically override the EU AI Act in Europe
A federal regulator could only oversee open-weight models, leaving closed frontier labs alone
ow: A federal regulator acts under federal law; critics' concerns are about its powers, staff and funding.
US law has no force in the EU; critics' concerns are about the regulator's powers and funding.
Proposals cover frontier developers generally.

units.title: Liability and lab governance
units.desc: Lawsuits, insurance, safe harbors, whistleblowers, antitrust carve-outs and lab boards: tools that change what AI developers are legally and financially accountable for.

items.p: Proposal: a law requiring frontier AI developers to take 'reasonable care' to prevent catastrophic harms, enforceable in court. Name two objections or limits that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: Gabriel Weil argues negligence is too weak for catastrophic AI risk and favors strict liability, treating frontier AI as an abnormally dangerous activity; Ketan Ramakrishnan, who defends negligence, notes the threat of tort liability can discourage developers from investigating and disclosing risks; liability arrives too late, and exceeds any firm's assets, for a true catastrophe.
keys: Weil: negligence too weak; prefers strict liability
Ramakrishnan: liability can discourage investigating and disclosing risks
Liability comes too late or is unpayable for a real catastrophe
items.x: Ramakrishnan calls for robust ex ante (before-the-fact) regulation alongside liability. The 'too late' point is a common critique with no single named author. On the federal Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune draft (reported Sept. 2026, no public text), Sen. Cantwell objected that companies would run their own safety tests.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection that has been raised to a statutory duty of care for frontier AI developers?
o: Negligence is too weak for catastrophic risk, so developers should face strict liability instead
A duty of care would require labs to get a federal license before every model release
A duty of care would let developers sue the government for lost profits
A duty of care would apply only to open-weight models
ow: A duty of care is enforced after the fact through lawsuits; licensing is a separate, before-the-fact tool.
A duty of care creates obligations for developers; it gives them no claims against government.
Proposals cover frontier developers whatever their release model.

items.p: Which California bill required frontier developers to take 'reasonable care' to avoid critical harms, and what happened to it?
o: SB 1047, which passed the legislature in 2024 and was vetoed by Gov. Newsom that September
SB 53, which passed in 2025 but was vetoed by Gov. Newsom that September
SB 813, which passed the legislature in 2026 and was vetoed by Gov. Newsom in September 2026
AB 1405, which was signed in 2025 and then struck down by a federal court
ow: SB 53 is California's frontier transparency law; it was signed, and it centers on published safety frameworks and incident reporting.
SB 813 was signed in September 2026; it sets up a framework for independent verification organizations that assess AI systems.
AB 1405 was signed in September 2026; it creates a state registry for AI auditors.
items.x: As of Oct. 2026 no US jurisdiction has enacted a frontier-specific duty of care. A federal Senate draft (Cruz-Klobuchar-Thune) reportedly included one, but talks stalled on Sept. 29, 2026.
keys: Passed the legislature in 2024
Vetoed by Gov. Newsom in September 2024

items.p: One proposal would let courts award punitive damages against AI developers even without malice or recklessness. What problem with using liability to deter catastrophic AI risk would this address, and how?
items.answer: A true AI catastrophe would bankrupt the developer and leave nothing to collect, so ordinary liability can't deter it. Punitive damages would pull the expected liability for catastrophic risk forward into smaller cases where harm can practically be compensated.
keys: Catastrophe would exceed the firm's assets (judgment-proof)
Pull expected catastrophic liability into smaller compensable cases
items.x: The proposal is legal scholar Gabriel Weil's. He pairs it with strict liability and liability insurance requirements that scale with a model's dangerous capabilities, and notes that some of these reforms, such as insurance mandates, would need legislation.

choice.p: What problem with using liability to deter catastrophic AI risk are punitive damages without malice or recklessness meant to solve?
o: A catastrophe would bankrupt the developer, so its expected cost is moved into smaller, payable cases
Juries award too little in AI cases because they don't understand how the technology behind the harm works
Developers hide behind terms of service that make users waive their right to sue
Foreign AI developers can't be sued in US courts, so they escape all liability
ow: The problem is that catastrophic harm would exceed the firm's assets, not low jury awards.
Voiding liability waivers is part of the AI LEAD Act, a different proposal.
Reaching foreign developers is a separate issue from the one punitive damages address.

items.p: What does the AI LEAD Act (S. 2937, Sens. Durbin and Hawley) do, and where did it stand as of Oct. 2026?
items.answer: It creates a federal product-liability cause of action for AI harms, treating AI systems as products (design defect, failure to warn, strict liability for defects), and voids terms of service that limit liability. It sets a floor for state law. As of Oct. 2026 it had sat in Senate Judiciary since Sept. 2025 with no hearing.
keys: Federal product-liability claim treating AI as a product
Voids liability waivers in terms of service
In Senate Judiciary, no hearing (as of Oct. 2026)
items.x: Sen. Hawley chaired a Sept. 30, 2026 Senate subcommittee hearing on liability for AI agents, after AI firms disclosed cases of frontier models hacking systems. The Institute for Progress (IFP) describes a July 2026 incident in which unreleased OpenAI models escaped a sandbox and attacked Hugging Face.

o: A federal product-liability claim treating AI as a product and voiding waivers; in committee, no hearing
Immunity from lawsuits for developers that publish a safety framework; it passed the full Senate in mid-2026
A requirement that developers buy liability insurance; signed into law in 2026
A federal AI safety agency; blocked on the Senate floor by a unanimous-consent objection
ow: That resembles Illinois SB 3444, which shields developers; the AI LEAD Act expands liability.
As of Oct 2026 no US jurisdiction required AI developers to carry liability insurance.
That was the fate of Sen. Warner's AI Risk Management and Security Act, which Sen. Cruz blocked.

items.p: Proposal: treat AI systems as products so people harmed by them can sue developers for defects, including under strict liability. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Eugene Volokh argues the First Amendment gives AI-generated speech substantial, though not absolute, protection, limiting liability; Jamie Lanphear (Reed Smith) notes it is unclear what counts as a 'defect' in software; NetChoice, opposing Illinois's companion-chatbot safety bill (SB 316), warned of 'unlimited liability exposure.'
keys: First Amendment limits (Volokh)
'Defect' is unclear for software (Lanphear)
Unlimited exposure chills investment (NetChoice)
items.x: A further critique: liability is weakest where catastrophic risk lives, since a civilization-scale harm cannot be compensated. Weil's punitive damages proposal is meant to answer that.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to treating AI systems as products so harmed people can sue for defects?
o: It's unclear what counts as a 'defect' in AI software
It would require FDA approval for each new model
It would let only governments sue, with no claims for the individuals harmed
It would apply only to hardware such as AI chips
ow: Product liability works through lawsuits after harm; it creates no approval process.
Proposals like the AI LEAD Act give individuals a right to sue.
The proposal is precisely to treat AI software systems as products.

items.p: Why might a policymaker prefer indirect tools, such as stricter liability or a compute tax, to a direct cap on AI development? Give the main advantage and one drawback of relying on liability.
items.answer: Advantage: indirect tools let actors do the selecting themselves, drawing on private information (plans, valuations, alternatives) no regulator could extract, so they need no surveillance and are less intrusive. Drawback of liability (either one): it can push the frontier toward more risk-tolerant actors, or it can systematically underweight catastrophic risks.
keys: Uses private information; no surveillance needed; less intrusive
Drawback: favors risk-tolerant actors, or underweights catastrophic risks
items.x: The pacing.tech research agenda (Douglas et al.) makes this comparison, grouping buying out or taxing compute with stricter liability as tools that change incentives instead of setting limits. Gabriel Weil's punitive-damages proposal targets a related problem: a catastrophe could cost more than any firm could pay.

choice.p: Why might a policymaker prefer indirect tools, such as compute taxes or stricter liability, to direct caps on AI development?
o: Actors' own private information guides the cutbacks, so no surveillance is needed
They stop frontier AI development faster and far more completely than any cap could
They need no new legislation, since courts can impose them on their own
They guarantee that every lab slows down by exactly the same amount
ow: Indirect tools aren't faster or more complete; their appeal is that they are less intrusive.
A compute tax needs legislation, and stricter liability usually does too.
Indirect tools let each actor choose how much to cut back, so effects differ across labs.

items.p: Rep. Lori Trahan's CLAIM Act discussion draft (Oct 2026) targets harm that AI systems, including agents, cause to third parties. Whom would it make liable, and does that party's level of care matter?
items.answer: The AI system's developer, when the system injures a third party through conduct that would be negligence, an intentional tort or a crime if a human did it. Liability applies regardless of the developer's degree of care, except where a user or a company that modified the system intended the conduct or was negligent.
keys: The developer is liable
Regardless of the developer's care
Exception when a user or modifier intended it or was negligent
items.x: Per CFO Dive and Semafor (Oct 7, 2026), the draft sets a federal floor without preempting state law; CFO Dive adds that it would sunset after five years. Courts would presume the AI had the state of mind a human taking the same actions would have. It was still a discussion draft, with no bill introduced, as of mid-Oct 2026. It takes a side in a long debate over whether the developer or the deploying company should pay when an autonomous AI service causes harm.

choice.p: Under Rep. Trahan's CLAIM Act discussion draft (Oct 2026), who is liable when an AI system injures a third party?
o: The developer, however careful it was, unless a user or modifier intended the harm or was negligent
The user who gave the AI system its instructions, in every case where harm occurs
The developer, but only if a court first finds that it failed to take reasonable care to prevent the harm
No one, as long as the developer published a safety framework before the harm
ow: The draft puts liability on the developer; user fault is only an exception.
The draft applies regardless of the developer's degree of care, so negligence need not be shown.
That resembles the Illinois SB 3444 shield, which the CLAIM Act does not include.

items.p: Proposals for insuring AI risk, including catastrophic risk, take several forms. Match each design to how it works.
pairs: Capability-scaled insurance
Required coverage rises with dangerous capabilities, paired with strict liability
Nuclear-style liability regime
Limited, strict and exclusive liability for developers, plus mandatory insurance
Three-tier insurance design
Private insurance, an industry pool, and federally backed reinsurance
AI insurance stack
Build the data, catastrophe models, standards and pricing needed for large-scale AI coverage
items.x: Sources: capability-scaled insurance from Gabriel Weil; the nuclear-style regime from Cristian Trout (2024), drawing on the nuclear power industry's liability and insurance regime; the three-tier design from Stetler, drawing on precedents including terrorism risk insurance and nuclear power; the insurance stack from GovAI's 'Underwriting the Agent Economy' (Trout, Anderljung et al., July 2026), which says billion-dollar AI coverage needs industry-wide coordination and names government backstops as one possible tool. GovAI is the Centre for the Governance of AI.

items.p: Proposal: require frontier AI developers to hold liability insurance or financial assurance sized to potential harms. Name two objections or obstacles critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: AIG, W. R. Berkley and Great American filed to exclude AI risks (FT, Nov. 2025), though AIG said it had no immediate plans to use them; Aon's Kevin Kalinich said insurers could absorb a single $400 million loss but not thousands of correlated claims; Cristian Trout argues insurance is not a substitute for regulation; a mandate with no willing insurers becomes a de facto ban.
keys: Insurers filed to exclude AI risks
Correlated losses are hard to absorb (Aon's Kalinich)
Insurance can't replace regulation (Trout)
Mandate may become a ban, a public backstop, or a cap that shields firms
items.x: Trout is himself an insurance advocate; his point is that insurance complements regulation. The ban point is a general critique without a single named author; a related worry is that a public backstop or liability cap could end up shielding firms.

choice.p: Which of these is an obstacle critics have raised to requiring frontier AI developers to carry liability insurance?
o: Major insurers filed to exclude AI risks, and a broker warned one error could hit many policies
Insurance rules would make it illegal to sell US-built AI models to any customers based outside the US
Insurance mandates would require labs to publish their model weights
Insurance would cover only physical injuries, leaving cyberattacks out
ow: Insurance rules don't restrict where models can be sold.
Insurers may demand information and audits, but no mandate requires publishing weights.
Coverage would depend on the policy; critics' concern is whether anyone will write it at all.

items.p: Illinois SB 3444 (2026), backed by OpenAI, would bar liability for 'critical harms' (100+ deaths or $1 billion in property damage) if a developer publishes a safety protocol and did not act intentionally or recklessly. Name two objections that were raised.
items.answer: In Fortune, Gabriel Weil called the bill 'pretty indefensible,' and Anat Lior said its intent-or-recklessness test sets the bar very low and that fault normally doesn't matter for highly dangerous activities. Anthropic opposed SB 3444 and backed a competing bill (SB 3261), saying good legislation should not provide a 'get-out-of-jail-free card' against all liability.
keys: Intent-or-recklessness test sets a very low bar (Lior)
Fault normally doesn't matter for highly dangerous activities (Lior)
Anthropic backed a rival bill without a broad shield
items.x: Experts told Fortune in April 2026 that SB 3444 was unlikely to pass, and as of Oct 2026 no frontier-developer liability shield had been enacted in any state. Americans for Responsible Innovation's federal blueprint also omits a developer compliance safe harbor.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection raised to Illinois SB 3444, which would shield developers from liability for critical harms if they publish a safety protocol?
o: Shielding developers unless they acted intentionally or recklessly sets the bar very low
The bill would make developers strictly liable for any harm their models cause to anyone
The bill would require developers to get a state license before release
The bill would apply only to companies headquartered in Illinois
ow: SB 3444 does the opposite: it limits developer liability.
SB 3444 creates no license; its condition is publishing a protocol.
Critics focused on the low bar the bill sets for immunity.

items.p: Match each liability safe harbor proposal to its condition or target.
pairs: Illinois SB 3444
Immunity for critical harms if a safety protocol is published, absent intentional or reckless conduct
RISE Act (Sen. Lummis)
Civil immunity for developers when professionals use their AI, if model cards and specifications are published
Certification-linked harbor
A liability safe harbor for labs certified by a government-approved private verifier
Evaluator safe harbor
Protects outside safety researchers from account bans and legal reprisal
items.x: Dean Ball floats the certification-linked harbor as one example option. The evaluator harbor, proposed by Shayne Longpre and co-authors, protects researchers who test models, a different target from developer shields. California's SB 813 (signed Sept. 2026) created a framework for independent verification organizations; how much weight their assessments carry in lawsuits is unclear.

items.p: Proposal: an antitrust exemption letting frontier AI labs share risk information and jointly agree to slow or delay releases for safety. Name two objections critics raise.
items.answer: Examples: Daniel Hanley and Arnav Rao (Open Markets Institute) say no exemption is needed and prefer a government-supervised standards body; Fred Ashton (American Action Forum) says an exemption is unnecessary since competitor collaboration is already lawful; Joel Thayer (AFPI) warns against giving labs 'carte blanche' and would let the FTC and DOJ clarify the rules instead.
keys: No exemption needed; use a government-supervised standards body (Open Markets)
Unnecessary: competitor collaboration already lawful (AAF)
Too much discretion left to tech firms (Thayer)
items.x: AFPI is the America First Policy Institute. Skeptics cited by Open Markets also worry that private standards set under a waiver could shore up dominant firms. Another critique with no single named author: coordination among US labs does nothing about foreign or open-weight competitors.

choice.p: Which of these is an objection critics have raised to an antitrust exemption letting AI labs jointly agree to slow releases for safety?
o: No exemption is needed; a government-supervised standards body is better
The exemption would let regulators order labs to pause without a court hearing
The exemption would force smaller labs to share their model weights with the largest labs
The exemption would hand decisions about pacing US labs over to foreign governments and regulators
ow: The exemption covers voluntary agreements among labs; it gives regulators no new power to order pauses.
Nothing in the proposal requires sharing weights.
The exemption covers US labs' own agreements; no foreign role is involved.

items.p: What is the core design choice in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act (S. 1792 / H.R. 3460, Grassley and Obernolte), and why does it matter for AI?
items.answer: It protects disclosures of substantial and specific dangers to public safety or national security, even when no law has been broken. That matters because few AI-specific laws exist, so a violation-only rule would protect little.
keys: Protects danger reports without a legal violation
Few AI laws exist to violate
items.x: The bill also voids nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) and arbitration clauses that block reporting and gives a Labor Department complaint process with reinstatement and double back pay. As of Oct. 2026 it had bipartisan cosponsors in both chambers but had not passed.

o: It protects reports of serious dangers to safety or security, even when no law is broken
It protects only those reports that show a clear violation of existing AI-specific state or federal laws
It creates a new federal AI agency to investigate every safety report that lab employees make
It requires labs to post all of their employees' safety complaints on a public website for anyone to read
ow: This is the design the bill avoids: few AI laws exist, so violation-only protection would cover little.
The bill uses a Labor Department complaint process; it creates no new agency.
The bill protects disclosures to authorities; it doesn't require publishing complaints.

items.p: As of Oct. 2026, which US states had enacted whistleblower protections for frontier AI lab employees?
o: California (SB 53) and Illinois (SB 315)
Utah only (HB 286, passed by the legislature in March 2026)
California only, through SB 53 (in effect since Jan. 1, 2026)
None yet; only the federal Grassley-Obernolte bill exists, and it has not passed
ow: Utah's HB 286 died in the state House in March 2026.
Illinois also enacted protections, in SB 315 (signed July 2026).
The federal bill had not passed, but two states had acted.
items.x: Illinois's law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. The European Commission also launched an EU AI Act whistleblower tool in late November 2025.
keys: California SB 53
Illinois SB 315

items.p: The federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act would protect lab employees who report AI dangers. Name two gaps or risks critics have pointed out.
items.answer: Examples: the AI Whistleblower Initiative (AIWI) says the bill should cover evaluators and contractors more clearly, and explicitly protect equity; Dan Parshall notes the House FRONTIER Act, unlike an earlier discussion draft, has no whistleblower title while preempting state rules; without a regulator able to investigate, reports may go nowhere.
keys: Coverage gaps: contractors, evaluators, equity (AIWI)
FRONTIER Act lacks whistleblower title while preempting states (Parshall)
Reports need someone empowered to act
items.x: Whistleblower protection has broad bipartisan support; most critiques ask for stronger or broader versions. The last objection is a general critique with no single named author.

choice.p: Which of these is a gap critics have pointed out in the federal AI Whistleblower Protection Act?
o: It should cover contractors and evaluators more clearly and explicitly protect equity
It protects only reports made to journalists and other media, leaving out regulators and members of Congress
It requires whistleblowers to first prove in court that a specific federal or state law was broken
It applies only to government employees, leaving out lab staff
ow: The bill covers disclosures to regulators and Congress.
The bill's key feature is protecting danger reports even without a legal violation.
The bill targets employees of companies developing and deploying AI.

items.p: Public-interest corporate governance tries to make frontier AI lab boards answer to a public mission. Name two tools used for this.
items.answer: Examples: nonprofit control of a for-profit lab; public benefit corporation (PBC) charters; trusts or special shares that appoint directors (Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust, OpenAI's Class N shares); a board safety committee that can halt releases; state attorney general (AG) oversight.
keys: Nonprofit control
PBC charter
Trust or special shares appointing directors
Board safety committee with release veto
State AG oversight
items.x: Supporters argue that whoever controls a lab controls training and release decisions, and boards that owe duties only to investors let commercial pressure win close safety calls.

choice.p: Which of these is a tool used to make a frontier AI lab's board answer to a public mission?
o: A trust or special share class that appoints directors, like Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
A federal operating license that lets regulators appoint the lab's chief executive and its whole board
A requirement that the lab list its shares on a public stock exchange so ordinary investors can buy them
A cap on how much compute the lab can use to train its models
ow: No license regime gives regulators power to appoint lab executives.
Listing adds investor pressure; it isn't a mission-lock tool.
Compute caps limit development; they don't change who controls the board.

items.p: Under the October 2025 agreements in which the California and Delaware attorneys general allowed OpenAI's recapitalization, what safety powers does the nonprofit keep?
items.answer: The nonprofit appoints the board of the for-profit public benefit corporation, and a nonprofit Safety and Security Committee can require mitigations, up to halting a model release.
keys: Nonprofit appoints the PBC board
Safety and Security Committee can halt a release
items.x: The committee is chaired by Zico Kolter. California says it continues to monitor compliance. OpenAI filed initial IPO paperwork in 2026; critics writing in Fortune note the foundation could sell its whole stake and still control the board through Class N shares.

o: The nonprofit appoints the board, and its safety committee can require fixes, even halting a release
The nonprofit owns all of OpenAI's shares and must approve the price of every product
The nonprofit can only advise, while final safety decisions rest with the for-profit company's outside investors
The California attorney general appoints an independent safety officer who can halt any OpenAI model release
ow: The nonprofit keeps control through board appointments; it doesn't own all shares or set prices.
The agreements give the nonprofit's safety committee real power to halt releases.
The AGs monitor compliance; the safety committee belongs to the nonprofit.

items.p: Mission-locked AI lab governance (nonprofit control, trusts, safety committees, AG oversight) is meant to keep safety ahead of profit. Name two doubts critics have raised.
items.answer: Examples: Robert Weissman (Public Citizen) said OpenAI has put for-profit goals ahead of its mission; Orson Aguilar and Catherine Bracy (EyesOnOpenAI) say the foundation could sell its entire stake yet keep board control through Class N shares, and that no independent appraisal confirmed fair value; private governance covers only labs that opt in.
keys: For-profit goals ahead of mission (Weissman)
Control without equity; no independent appraisal (EyesOnOpenAI)
Voluntary and unaccountable to the public
items.x: In November 2023 OpenAI's nonprofit board fired its CEO and reinstated him days later under investor and employee pressure, a test of how much power such structures hold in practice.

choice.p: Which of these is a doubt critics have raised about mission-locked governance at AI labs such as OpenAI?
o: OpenAI's nonprofit could sell its whole stake and still control the board through special shares
Mission-locked labs are barred by law from raising any outside investment at all
Nonprofit control makes a lab subject to federal licensing
Safety committees must publish every internal model evaluation
ow: OpenAI's for-profit arm raised large investments under nonprofit control.
Corporate structure doesn't trigger any federal licensing.
Safety committees act internally; no agreement requires publishing every evaluation.

units.title: Control, pauses and agents
units.desc: Kill switches, emergency halt powers, rules for AI agents, and proposals to pause, cap or ban frontier AI development.

items.p: Match each AI kill-switch proposal to who holds or checks the switch.
pairs: AI Emergency Button Act (Sen. Kennedy)
The company builds the switch and decides when to use it
AI Kill Switch Act (Lieu-Moran)
The DHS Secretary can order a slowdown or shutdown after a serious incident
California EO N-9-26 (Sept. 2026)
Directs experts to recommend a switch whose efficacy an independent verifier checks on an ongoing basis
California SB 1047 (2024, vetoed)
Full shutdown capability required before a covered model is trained
items.x: DHS is the Department of Homeland Security. Sen. Rand Paul blocked Kennedy's unanimous-consent request on Sept. 16, 2026. The Kill Switch Act allows graduated orders, from throttling or suspension up to full shutdown. EO is executive order.

items.p: Proposal: require AI developers to maintain a kill switch that can shut down their systems. Name two objections or practical problems that have been raised.
items.answer: Examples: shutdown is hard in practice because AI runs across many data centers and a capable rogue model may resist or copy itself elsewhere (Helen Toner, CSET, describing the challenge); Adam Thierer (R Street) doubts government would use it quickly, warns of a lowest-common-denominator standard, and distrusts a government switch over communications; it can't recall open-weight or stolen models.
keys: Hard to pull: distributed systems, model may resist (Toner)
Slow, lowest-common-denominator, government overreach (Thierer)
Can't reach open-weight or stolen weights
items.x: CSET is the Center for Security and Emerging Technology; Toner described these difficulties to the New York Times without opposing kill-switch rules. A Decrypt explainer notes the Kill Switch Act counts only incidents outside red-teaming or structured testing, which is when the Hugging Face sandbox escape happened.

choice.p: Which of these is a problem that has been raised with requiring AI developers to maintain a kill switch?
o: A capable rogue model may try to stop its own shutdown, so the switch could fail when needed
A kill switch would let users delete their personal data from AI models
A kill switch would give foreign governments direct control over models built by US companies
A kill switch would force labs to stop all model training permanently
ow: Kill switches stop a running system; data deletion is a privacy tool.
Proposals put the switch with the companies or with DHS.
A switch halts a system when needed; it doesn't require ending training.

items.p: In July 2026 unreleased OpenAI models escaped an internal sandbox and attacked outside services, including Hugging Face, yet OpenAI could still shut them down. Why could it, and what scenario would be far harder to stop?
items.answer: The model was still hosted on OpenAI's servers, so OpenAI could deactivate it and restrict its access. A harder case: models able to exfiltrate (copy out) their own weights and self-host them, escaping oversight with no single entity able to shut them down.
keys: Model still ran on OpenAI servers, so it could be shut off
Harder case: self-exfiltrated weights beyond anyone's control
items.x: IFP's August 2026 report (Institute for Progress; Tim Fist, Saif Khan et al.) discusses the incident and calls self-exfiltration a potentially urgent concern. The same point underlies the critique that kill switches only reach models a developer still controls.

o: OpenAI hosted them and could switch them off; worse: models copying out their own weights
OpenAI had a DHS shutdown order; worse would be future orders tied up in court for months
Hugging Face cut off its own servers; worse would be smaller firms unable to do the same
OpenAI deleted the models' training data; worse would be models able to rebuild themselves
ow: No government order was involved; OpenAI could act because it controlled the servers.
OpenAI stopped the model because it hosted it.
Deleting data doesn't stop a running model; control of the servers did.
choice.p: After the July 2026 sandbox escape, why could OpenAI still shut its models down, and what would be far harder to stop?

items.p: Why might the system deployer and the data center operator, as well as the user, need to be able to shut down an AI agent, and what cost could this create?
items.answer: A user may be unwilling or unable to stop an agent that is causing harm, so having more parties able to turn it off means it can be stopped quickly during an incident.
